question: Which context paragraph is best for a rendering ADR?
options: We chose ISR because it is the modern approach recommended by our framework.
Search brings 70% of visitors. Product data changes twice a day; account pages are per user. Rendering is billed per request.
The team likes Next.js and wants to try the App Router.
explanation: The context lists forces (SEO share, freshness, personalization, cost) neutrally, so a reader can check the decision against them. The others argue for a tool or say nothing.

question: A route shows each user's saved searches, is not indexed and changes on every visit. Which model contradicts the briefing?
explanation: ISR serves one shared, cached HTML to everyone. Per-user data must be rendered per request on the server or fetched on the client.

question: Your ADR chose ISR with a 5-minute revalidate for product pages. Which line belongs in the negative consequences?
options: Pages are served from the CDN.
Search engines see the full content.
The build no longer grows with the number of products.
A price can be up to 5 minutes old, so the cart re-checks prices on the server.
explanation: The stale window is the price paid for ISR. Recording it, and what compensates for it, is what makes the trade-off visible.

question: Why list "SSR for every route" as an alternative when the team never planned it?
options: Because "one model everywhere" is what someone will propose later, and the record should already say which fact rules it out
Because every ADR must reject SSR
It should not be listed; only seriously planned options belong in an ADR
explanation: The uniform option is the most common challenge to a per-route map. Writing down why it lost (cost on deploy-only pages, for example) saves the debate later.
